chapter.name: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

questions.q: Kabir's doha praises the soop for keeping what is worth keeping and letting the worthless part blow away. A farmer tips 20 kg of threshed rice from a soop in a strong breeze: 16 kg of clean grain lands near her feet and 4 kg of husk is carried farther. Next morning, in only a faint breeze, she tips another 20 kg from the same harvest and only 1 kg is carried farther. What is in the heap near her feet the second time?
questions.a: About 16 kg of grain mixed with about 3 kg of husk, as the faint breeze carried off too little husk
o: About 16 kg of grain mixed with about 3 kg of husk, as the faint breeze carried off too little husk
About 19 kg of clean grain, because any breeze sorts the grain fully and only the time taken to do it changes
About 15 kg of grain and 4 kg of husk, because the faint breeze carried off 1 kg of the heavier grain instead
About 16 kg of clean grain, because the extra 3 kg is husk that fell beside the heap, not in it

questions.q:
Sonu's grandmother has a tin of puffed rice mixed with uncooked rice grains. Sonu says, 'Let us beat it on a wooden log, the way farmers thresh wheat.'
(a) Explain why threshing cannot separate this mixture.
(b) Name a method that can, and say which part lands where.
questions.a: (a) Threshing separates grains that are attached to stalks, by beating. Here both parts are already loose and nothing is attached, so beating only crushes the puffed rice and does not sort the two. (b) Winnowing: the light puffed rice is carried farther by the moving air, while the heavier rice grains fall close by.
s: Part (a): threshing frees grains attached to stalks; nothing here is attached
Part (b): winnowing, puffed rice carried away, rice grains fall near

questions.q: A farmer stands on a raised platform and slowly tips threshed rice from a soop. A steady wind blows from east to west. Where will most of the husk land compared with the grains?
questions.a: Farther to the west than the grains, because the light husk is carried along by the wind
o: Farther to the west than the grains, because the light husk is carried along by the wind
Farther to the east than the grains, because the light husk drifts back against the wind
Directly below the tray, because the husk is heavier than the grains and drops straight down
In the same heap as the grains, because wind cannot sort two solids that are mixed together

questions.q:
Assertion (A): After threshing harvested wheat on a log, the farmer still has to winnow the grains.
Reason (R): Threshing separates the grains from the stalks, but the separated grains get mixed with piles of husk.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
For each heap below, name the method that should be used on it first, and give the difference between the components that the method depends on.
P: 1 kg of rice with six small stones in it.
Q: 1 kg of threshed rice with its husk still mixed all through it.
R: Bundles of dried bajra stalks with the grains still attached.
questions.a: P: handpicking, because the stones are few and differ from the rice in size, colour and shape (they are heavy, so wind would not remove them). Q: winnowing, because the husk is lighter than the grains and is far too much to pick by hand. R: threshing, because the grains are attached to the stalks and must be beaten off before anything else can be done.
s: P: handpicking, few stones differing in size, colour or shape
Q: winnowing, lighter husk against heavier grain
R: threshing, grains attached to stalks freed by beating

questions.q: A grocer spills a large scoop of light, dry moong husk flakes into a 10 kg sack of whole moong. Picking out every flake would take a whole day. Which method should he use instead?
questions.a: Winnowing, as moving air carries off the light flakes and the moong falls close by
o: Winnowing, as moving air carries off the light flakes and the moong falls close by
Threshing, as beating the sack on a log frees the flakes stuck to each moong
Handpicking, as it is always the best method when there are very many particles
Winnowing, as moving air carries off the heavy moong and the flakes fall close by

questions.q:
Handpicking uses differences in size, colour or shape. For each plate, say which difference makes the unwanted bits easy to spot, and why the other two differences do not help.
(a) A few small white stones, the same size and shape as the grains, in a plate of black urad dal.
(b) A few small round white pebbles, as big as the grains, in a plate of long white rice.
questions.a: (a) Colour: the stones are white against black dal, while their size and shape match the grains. (b) Shape: the pebbles are round and the rice grains are long, while their colour and size are the same.
s: Part (a): colour, as size and shape are the same
Part (b): shape, as colour and size are the same

questions.q: A farmer winnows 25 kg of threshed bajra in which 12% of the mass is husk. If the wind carries away all of the husk, the heap that forms close to her feet has a mass of ___ kg.

In Nani's courtyard, the family beat 40 kg of harvested wheat stalks and collected 18 kg of loose grain mixed with husk. After using soops in the afternoon breeze, 15 kg of grain was left. A 500 g handful of this grain held 12 small stones; assume the stones are spread evenly. Most of the stones are smaller than the wheat grains. One person can handpick about 120 stones in an hour, and four family members are free for the next 30 minutes. Mama's sieve lets small stones fall through: sieving all 15 kg takes 1 person-hour in total (they have enough sieves to share the work), removes 300 of the stones, and lets 450 g of broken grain fall through with them, which is thrown away.
(a) Name the method that produced the 18 kg of loose grain and husk from the stalks.
(b) What did the soops remove, what was its mass, and which property let the breeze carry it?
(c) Estimate the number of stones in the 15 kg of grain and the time four people need to handpick them all.
(d) Nani wants to handpick every stone. Mama wants to sieve first and then handpick only the stones the sieve leaves. Compare the two plans in person-hours and grain lost, and say which you would choose in the 30 minutes they have.
questions.a: (a) Threshing. (b) Husk, 18 - 15 = 3 kg; it is lighter than the grains, so moving air carries it away. (c) 15,000 g / 500 g = 30 handfuls, 30 x 12 = 360 stones; 360 / 120 = 3 person-hours, so about 45 minutes for four people. (d) Nani's plan: 3 person-hours (45 minutes for four, 15 minutes more than they have) and no grain lost. Mama's plan: 1 person-hour of sieving plus 60 stones left / 120 = 0.5 person-hour of picking, 1.5 person-hours in all (about 22.5 minutes for four, inside the 30 minutes), but 450 g of grain (3%) is thrown away. A full-mark answer chooses either plan and uses both sides: Mama's fits the time at the cost of 450 g of grain; Nani's wastes no grain but runs 15 minutes over.
s: Part (a): threshing
Part (b): 3 kg of husk, removed because it is lighter
Part (c): about 360 stones, about 45 minutes for four (3 person-hours)
Part (d): 3 against 1.5 person-hours (45 against about 22.5 minutes) and 0 against 450 g of grain lost, with a justified choice

questions.q: A farmer winnows 30 kg of threshed ragi on a windy afternoon, and the heap at her feet weighs 26 kg. A 100 g sample from this heap still contains 2 g of husk. About how much husk is still in the heap, and what does it tell her?
questions.a: About 520 g; one pass did not carry all the light husk away, so a second winnowing is worth doing
o: About 520 g; one pass did not carry all the light husk away, so a second winnowing is worth doing
About 520 g; the husk left behind must be heavier than the grain, so winnowing again is useless
About 52 g; so little is left that it can be removed only by picking each flake out by hand
About 2 kg; the wind carried off 4 kg, so roughly half as much husk must still be left lying in the heap

questions.q: True or False? A farmer winnows 10 kg of threshed wheat in which 15% of the mass is husk. The heap carried farther from her feet weighs 2.5 kg, so the wind must have carried some grain away along with the husk. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The husk is only 15% of 10 kg = 1.5 kg. The far heap weighs 2.5 kg, so at least 1 kg of it is not husk: some grain (for example light, broken grains in a strong wind) was carried along with the lighter husk instead of falling close by.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: husk is only 1.5 kg, so the extra 1 kg in the far heap must be grain carried by the wind

questions.q:
Statement 1: Winnowing can be done indoors in front of a running fan, because blowing air separates the lighter husk just as wind does.
Statement 2: Threshing separates husk from grains by letting the wind carry the husk away.
Statement 3: Handpicking is convenient when the unwanted particles are few and can easily be picked by hand.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Neha says, 'Handpicking uses differences in size, colour and shape, so it is the best method for cleaning every grain mixture, even a big pile of threshed wheat full of husk.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that handpicking works on differences in size, colour and shape. She is wrong that it suits every mixture: it is convenient only when the unwanted particles are few and easily picked. A big pile of husk is better removed by winnowing.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: handpicking uses size, colour and shape
Wrong part: only convenient for a few, easily picked particles; husk piles need winnowing

questions.q:
Match each farm or kitchen task in Column I with the method it uses in Column II.
Column I
1. Picking a few stones out of a plate of rajma
2. Beating bundles of dried mustard stalks on a wooden log
3. Tipping threshed jowar from a soop in a breeze
4. A machine that frees grain from stalks and removes husk in one go
Column II
a. Thresher
b. Handpicking
c. Threshing
d. Winnowing

A sack holds 25 kg of rice, with about 3 kg of small stones spread all through it.
(a) Is handpicking a convenient way to clean this sack?
(b) Give a reason using the condition the chapter states for handpicking.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) Handpicking is convenient only when the particles to be removed are present in small quantities and can easily be picked; 3 kg of stones spread through 25 kg is far too many to pick one by one.
s: Part (a): not convenient
Part (b): handpicking suits only a small quantity of easily picked particles; 3 kg is a large quantity

questions.q:
Harvested paddy reaches a village courtyard as bundles of dried stalks, and the grain has a few small stones from the field mixed in it. By evening the family has clean rice ready to cook.
(a) Name the three methods they use, and say which one must come first.
(b) For threshing and for winnowing, state the difference between the components that the method depends on.
(c) State why handpicking suits the stones.
(d) Explain why the family does not handpick the husk as well.
(e) Explain why winnowing cannot be done before threshing.
questions.a: (a) Threshing, winnowing and handpicking; threshing must come first. (Winnowing and handpicking may be done in either order, though the few stones are easier to see once the husk has gone.) (b) Threshing: the grains are attached to the stalks and are knocked off by beating. Winnowing: the husk is lighter and the grains heavier, so moving air carries the husk away. (c) The stones are few and differ from rice in size, colour and shape, so they are easily picked. (d) The husk is present in piles, far too much to pick one by one; handpicking is convenient only for small quantities, and the wind removes the light husk quickly. (e) Before threshing, the grains are still attached to the stalks, so there is no loose mixture of grain and husk for the wind to sort.
s: Part (a): threshing, winnowing, handpicking, with threshing first
Part (b): attached grains freed by beating; lighter husk blown off heavier grain
Part (c): stones few, different in size, colour and shape
Part (d): husk too plentiful to pick; wind removes the lighter husk
Part (e): grains still on the stalks, no loose grain-husk mixture

questions.q: Which pairing of a method with the difference it depends on is NOT correct?
questions.a: Threshing: the difference in weight between grain and husk
o: Threshing: the difference in weight between grain and husk
Handpicking: the difference in colour between stones and rice
Winnowing: the difference in weight between husk and grain
Handpicking: the difference in shape between peppercorns and rice

questions.q:
Ritu rubs roasted peanuts between her palms. The bowl now holds peanuts, loose papery skins and a few broken pieces of hard shell, each about as heavy as a peanut. She blows gently over the bowl.
(a) Which part is blown away, and which parts stay in the bowl?
(b) Name the method she should use next for the shell pieces, and say why blowing cannot remove them.
questions.a: (a) The light skins are blown away; the heavier peanuts and shell pieces stay. (b) Handpicking: the shell pieces are few and differ from the peanuts in shape and colour. Being about as heavy as the peanuts, they fall with them, so blowing air cannot separate them.
s: Part (a): skins blown away, peanuts and shell pieces stay
Part (b): handpicking; shell pieces as heavy as peanuts, so air cannot separate them

questions.q: Kabir's grandfather winnows a basket of wheat that has a few small stones in it. After winnowing, the stones are still in the grain. Explain why winnowing could not remove them, and say how they should be removed.
questions.a: Winnowing works because the wind carries away the lighter component while the heavier one falls close by. The stones are heavy, at least as heavy as the grains, so they fall with the grains and are not blown away. Since they are few and differ in colour and shape, they should be handpicked.
s: Winnowing separates only by lighter versus heavier with moving air
Stones are heavy, fall with the grains, so the wind cannot carry them off
Handpicking named as the method, because the stones are few and look different

questions.q: Write a short situation, not about grain or husk, in which blowing air separates two dry solids. Name the part that is blown away and the part that stays, and give one reason why handpicking would be a poor choice in your situation.
questions.a: Example: a carpenter blows the fine, light wood shavings off a tray of small iron screws. The light shavings fly off while the heavier screws stay on the tray. Picking out hundreds of tiny shavings one by one would take far too long, since handpicking suits only a few, easily picked particles.
s: A setting with two dry solids, one clearly lighter
Lighter part blown away, heavier part stays, stated correctly
Handpicking rejected because the unwanted particles are many or tiny

questions.q:
A Class 6 group winnowed three equal samples of rice. Each sample weighed 2 kg and held 400 g of husk. Each was tipped from a soop once: in a closed room with no fan, in front of a running table fan, and outdoors in a light morning breeze. Husk still left in the rice afterwards: closed room 300 g, fan 60 g, breeze 100 g.
(a) What percentage of the husk did the fan remove, and which property of the husk let the moving air carry it?
(b) Explain why the closed room removed so little husk.
(c) Suppose each pass in the same breeze removes the same fraction of the husk still left as the first breeze pass did. How much husk would remain after a second pass in the breeze?
(d) A village wants each day's harvest cleaned the same day. The breeze blows only from 6 to 8 am, and one pass of a day's harvest takes about 1.5 hours, so a second breeze pass has to wait for the next morning. Fans can run in the afternoon, but the electricity for one pass costs Rs 40 a day. Should it plan on one pass in front of fans or two passes in the morning breeze? Justify using (a) and (c).
questions.a: (a) (400 - 60) / 400 = 85%; the husk is lighter than the grains, so moving air carries it away. (b) Winnowing needs wind or blown air; in still air the husk fell with the grains, so only 100 g (25%) was removed. (c) The first breeze pass removed 300 of 400 g, that is 75%; a second pass removes 75% of the 100 g left, leaving 25 g. (d) A real trade-off. Two breeze passes leave 25 g of husk against 60 g after one fan pass and cost nothing, but the second pass finishes only the next morning, so the rice waits a day. One fan pass finishes the same day but leaves more than twice as much husk (60 g against 25 g) and costs Rs 40 a day. A full-mark answer chooses one and weighs 25 g against 60 g with the day's wait against Rs 40. (One breeze pass followed by one fan pass the same afternoon, worked out, is also accepted.)
s: Part (a): 85%, husk is lighter
Part (b): still air cannot carry away the lighter husk
Part (c): 25 g left after the second pass
Part (d): a choice weighing 25 g against 60 g of husk with the next-day wait against Rs 40 a day

questions.q:
A farmers' group in Haryana must clean 5,400 kg of wheat. Manual method: 4 workers, each paid Rs 500 a day, beat the stalks on a log and then use soops, together finishing 300 kg of grain a day. Machine method: a thresher hired at Rs 2,400 a day, with 2 workers at Rs 500 a day each to feed it, finishes 1,800 kg a day.
(a) Explain why the manual team's beating on the log can go on in still air, but its soop work can go on only while the air is moving.
(b) How many days does each method take, and what is its total cost?
(c) If still air stops the manual soop work on 4 extra days, for which the workers are still paid, what do the manual method's days and cost become?
(d) Explain why the grain from the thresher needs no soop work afterwards, while the manual team's grain does.
(e) Suggest how the manual team could avoid losing the 4 still days without hiring the thresher, and explain why your idea works.
questions.a: (a) Beating is threshing: it knocks the grains off the stalks and needs no wind. The soops are used for winnowing, which needs wind or blown air to carry the lighter husk away from the heavier grain; in still air the two fall together. (b) Manual: 5,400 / 300 = 18 days, 18 x 4 x 500 = Rs 36,000. Machine: 5,400 / 1,800 = 3 days, 3 x (2,400 + 2 x 500) = Rs 10,200. (c) 18 + 4 = 22 days, costing 22 x 4 x 500 = Rs 44,000. (d) The thresher does threshing and winnowing at the same time, so its grain comes out already separated from the husk. (e) Blow air across the soops with a fan (or any blower): winnowing works with blown air as well as with wind, because it is the moving air that carries the lighter husk away.
s: Part (a): threshing needs only beating; winnowing needs moving air to carry the lighter husk
Part (b): 18 days, Rs 36,000; 3 days, Rs 10,200
Part (c): 22 days, Rs 44,000
Part (d): thresher threshes and winnows simultaneously
Part (e): a fan or blower, because blown air also winnows

questions.q:
Statement 1: A sieve can separate rice flour from the water it has been stirred into.
Statement 2: Sieving separates the parts of a solid-solid mixture by the difference in their particle size.
Statement 3: At construction sites, sieves hold back pebbles and stones while the sand passes through.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A shopkeeper finds whole mustard seeds (about 2 mm across) mixed into a tin of besan, whose particles are about 0.1 mm. He has two sieves, one with 0.2 mm holes and one with 3 mm holes.
(a) Which sieve will separate the two, and which part will he find on top of it?
(b) Explain why the other sieve fails.
questions.a: (a) The 0.2 mm sieve: the fine besan passes through and the mustard seeds stay on top. (b) The 3 mm holes are larger than both the besan particles and the seeds, so everything passes through together.
s: Part (a): 0.2 mm sieve, mustard seeds stay on top
Part (b): 3 mm holes larger than both, so both pass

questions.q: Mami sieves 2 kg of freshly ground atta and finds 150 g left on the sieve: bran flakes and a few small stones. She shakes these 150 g again on the same sieve for five more minutes. What will happen?
questions.a: Almost nothing passes, because all of it is bigger than the holes
o: Almost nothing passes, because all of it is bigger than the holes
The bran passes this time, because it has been shaken for longer
The stones pass, because no flour is left to block the holes now
About half passes, because each sieving lets half the solid through

questions.q:
Three sieves are tested: P has 0.2 mm holes, Q has 1 mm holes and R has 5 mm holes. A mixture contains fine flour (particles about 0.1 mm), bran flakes (about 1.5 mm), small stones (about 3 mm) and whole wheat grains (about 6 mm).
(a) What passes through P?
(b) What stays on R?
(c) What stays on Q?
(d) Can any one of P, Q or R separate the bran from the small stones? Explain.
(e) What hole size would you choose for a new sieve to separate bran from small stones?
questions.a: (a) Only the fine flour (0.1 mm is less than 0.2 mm). (b) Only the whole wheat grains (6 mm is more than 5 mm). (c) Bran, stones and wheat grains stay; only flour passes. (d) No: Q (1 mm) holds back both bran and stones, R (5 mm) lets both pass, and P holds both. (e) Any size between 1.5 mm and 3 mm, for example 2 mm, so the bran passes and the stones stay.
s: Part (a): flour only
Part (b): wheat grains only
Part (c): bran, stones and grains stay on Q
Part (d): none works, reason from hole sizes
Part (e): a hole size between 1.5 mm and 3 mm

questions.q: A sieve has holes 2 mm wide. It is shaken with 600 g of a mixture that holds 150 g of grains about 0.5 mm across, 250 g of grains about 1.5 mm across and 200 g of grains about 3 mm across. The mass that passes through the sieve is ___ g.

A mason in Bhopal has a 600 kg heap that holds 450 kg of fine sand (grains under 1 mm), 90 kg of gravel (pieces 4 to 8 mm) and 60 kg of pebbles (15 to 40 mm). She has two sieves: sieve A with 2 mm holes and sieve B with 10 mm holes. She needs 400 kg of fine sand only, for plastering, and 120 kg of sand and gravel together, with no pebbles, for concrete.
(a) Which component or components pass through sieve A?
(b) What percentage of the heap passes through sieve B?
(c) After she takes the 400 kg for plastering, how much sand and gravel together is left for concrete?
(d) Plan which sieve or sieves she should use, and in what order, to meet both needs. Justify.
questions.a: (a) Only the fine sand, because only its grains are smaller than 2 mm. (b) Sand and gravel pass: (450 + 90) / 600 = 90%. (c) 450 - 400 = 50 kg of sand plus 90 kg of gravel = 140 kg, which is more than the 120 kg needed. (d) Sieve the heap through B to hold back the pebbles, then sieve what passed through A: the 450 kg of fine sand passes, giving the 400 kg for plaster; the 90 kg of gravel left on A is mixed with the remaining 50 kg of sand for concrete. (Using A first and then B on what stays on A also works, if justified.)
s: Part (a): only the fine sand
Part (b): 90%
Part (c): 140 kg
Part (d): a two-sieve plan that keeps pebbles out of both and gives 400 kg of fine sand, justified by hole sizes

questions.q: At a building site, a worker throws shovelfuls of sand from a heap through a wire-mesh screen whose holes are about 5 mm wide. The heap contains sand grains under 1 mm and pebbles of 10 to 30 mm. What happens?
questions.a: Sand grains pass through the mesh, while the pebbles stay in front of it
o: Sand grains pass through the mesh, while the pebbles stay in front of it
Pebbles pass through the mesh, while the sand grains stay in front of it
Both pass through, since the mesh only slows the heavier pebbles down
Neither passes, since a mesh can work only on flour, not on sand

questions.q: True or False? A builder can separate pebbles from sand with a sieve, because the pebbles are bigger than the holes and the sand grains are smaller. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Sieving separates solids of different sizes: the small sand grains pass through the holes and the bigger pebbles stay on the sieve.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the parts differ in size, the holes lie between the two sizes

questions.q: A tea-stall owner spills sugar crystals into a jar of salt crystals of nearly the same size. He tries a fine sieve and then a coarse sieve, but neither separates them. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Sieving needs particles of different sizes, and these crystals are the same size
o: Sieving needs particles of different sizes, and these crystals are the same size
Sieving works only on solids that are mixed with water, not on dry crystals
One sieve's holes were too small and the other's too large; a medium sieve will work
The sugar has dissolved into the salt, so the crystals no longer have a size

questions.q: Arjun claims, 'Any sieve will separate any two dry solids, as long as you shake it for long enough.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Sieving works only when the two solids differ in particle size, and only when the holes are smaller than the bigger particles but larger than the smaller ones. Same-sized particles, or holes larger than both, give no separation however long you shake.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
The solids must differ in particle size
The hole size must lie between the two particle sizes; shaking longer does not change this

questions.q:
A ration-shop worker wants to remove broken rice bits (about 1 mm across) from whole rice grains (about 2 mm thick). She has three sieves, with holes of 0.5 mm, 1.5 mm and 3 mm.
(a) Which sieve should she use, and why?
(b) Say what goes wrong with each of the other two sieves.
questions.a: (a) The 1.5 mm sieve: its holes are larger than the broken bits but smaller than the whole grains, so the bits pass and the grains stay. (b) The 0.5 mm sieve holds back both, as both are bigger than its holes; the 3 mm sieve lets both through, as both are smaller than its holes.
s: Part (a): 1.5 mm, holes between the two sizes
Part (b): 0.5 mm keeps both, 3 mm passes both

questions.q:
Mami has 5 kg of freshly ground atta containing bran and a few small stones. With her fine sieve, 4.6 kg passes and 0.4 kg (0.35 kg of bran and 0.05 kg of stones) stays on top; this takes 25 minutes. With her coarse sieve, 4.85 kg passes and only 0.15 kg stays on top; this takes 8 minutes. Neither sieve lets any stones through.
(a) What percentage of the atta stayed on the fine sieve?
(b) What mass of bran passed through the coarse sieve into the flour?
(c) Explain why the coarse sieve let some bran through but held back every stone.
(d) Guests arrive in 15 minutes and she wants to make puris from bran-free flour. Which sieve should she use? Justify using the data.
questions.a: (a) 0.4 / 5 = 8%. (b) 4.85 - 4.6 = 0.25 kg of bran. (c) Its holes are larger than some bran flakes but smaller than the stones, so some bran passes while all stones stay. (d) This is a real trade-off, and a full-mark answer picks one side and uses both numbers: the fine sieve gives bran-free flour but needs 25 minutes, 10 minutes more than she has; the coarse sieve is ready in 8 minutes but leaves 0.25 kg of bran in the flour. For example: use the fine sieve and serve the puris about 10 minutes late, or use the coarse sieve and accept some bran.
s: Part (a): 8%
Part (b): 0.25 kg
Part (c): hole size larger than some bran, smaller than stones
Part (d): a choice that weighs 25 minutes against 0.25 kg of bran left

questions.q: In which case will sieving NOT separate the two solids?
questions.a: The holes of the sieve are larger than both kinds of particles
o: The holes of the sieve are larger than both kinds of particles
The holes are smaller than the pebbles but larger than the sand grains
The flour particles are finer than the holes and the bran is bigger
The gram flour is fine and the whole black gram is bigger than the holes

questions.q: A bag holds dried whole peas (about 7 mm across), rice grains (about 2 mm thick) and fine sand (about 0.5 mm). You have two sieves, one with 4 mm holes and one with 1 mm holes. Describe how you would get each of the three parts separately.
questions.a: Sieve the mixture through the 4 mm sieve: the peas stay on top, while rice and sand pass. Then sieve what passed through the 1 mm sieve: the rice stays on top and the fine sand passes through. Each step works because the holes are between the sizes of the parts being separated.
s: 4 mm sieve first: peas kept, rice and sand pass
1 mm sieve next: rice kept, sand passes
Each step justified by hole size lying between particle sizes

questions.q: Sieving and handpicking can both use a difference in size. Describe one situation where sieving is clearly the better choice, and give the reason.
questions.a: Removing bran from 10 kg of flour (or pebbles from a heap of sand). The unwanted particles are very many and small, so picking them one by one is not convenient; a sieve separates all of them at once by size.
s: A suitable situation with many small unwanted particles
Reason: handpicking suits only a few easily picked particles; a sieve treats the whole mixture at once

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When wheat flour is sieved, the bran stays on the sieve while the fine flour passes through.
Reason (R): Bran particles are smaller than the holes of the sieve.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: The mesh of Dadi's flour sieve has torn, leaving a gap the size of a fingertip at one edge. She sieves atta through it as usual. What will she find?
questions.a: Some bran and small stones get into the sieved flour through the gap
o: Some bran and small stones get into the sieved flour through the gap
The flour stops passing through the sieve because the gap is too big
The bran now passes through the small holes and the flour stays behind
The sieve works as before, because the size of the holes does not matter

questions.q: Write a short real-life situation, from a kitchen, a farm or a building site, in which a sieve is the right tool. Name the two solids, say which one passes through and which stays, and state the hole size needed compared with the two solids.
questions.a: Example: at a building site, a worker throws sand through a mesh with 5 mm holes. The sand grains (under 1 mm) pass through and the pebbles (over 10 mm) stay in front. The holes must be larger than the sand grains but smaller than the pebbles.
s: A real setting with two solids of different sizes
Which passes and which stays, stated correctly
Hole size placed between the two particle sizes

questions.q: The holes of a kitchen flour sieve are much smaller than the holes of a sieve used to clean sand at a building site. Give a reason for this difference.
questions.a: For sieving to work, the holes must be smaller than the bigger particles but larger than the smaller ones. Flour and bran are very fine, so the flour sieve needs tiny holes; sand and pebbles are much bigger, so the building sieve can have larger holes that still hold back pebbles.
s: Rule: holes must lie between the sizes of the two components
Applied: flour and bran are fine, sand and pebbles are coarse, so hole sizes differ

questions.q:
Shreya says, 'At a building site, sieving sand wastes time. The pebbles can simply be handpicked.' The site has two heaps of 2,000 kg of sand, with sand grains under 1 mm. Heap P contains 160 kg of pebbles of about 20 g each, the smallest about 10 mm across. Heap Q contains only 6 kg of large stones of about 100 g each. A worker can handpick about 10 pebbles or stones a minute, and sieving a whole heap takes one worker about 3 hours.
(a) For Heap P, what must be true of the sieve's holes compared with the sand grains and the pebbles?
(b) State the condition under which the chapter says handpicking is a convenient method.
(c) How many pebbles or stones does each heap contain, and how long would one worker take to handpick each heap clean? Give the times in hours and minutes.
(d) After sieving Heap P, a few flat pebbles had slipped through the holes on their edges. Which method suits these, and why?
(e) Judge Shreya's claim for each heap, using your answers.
questions.a: (a) The holes must be larger than 1 mm, so the sand passes, but smaller than 10 mm, so every pebble stays. (b) Handpicking is convenient when the particles to be removed are present in small quantities and can easily be picked by hand. (c) Heap P: 160,000 g / 20 g = 8,000 pebbles; 8,000 / 10 = 800 minutes = 13 hours 20 minutes. Heap Q: 6,000 g / 100 g = 60 stones; 60 / 10 = 6 minutes. (d) Handpicking: only a few pebbles are left, and they differ from sand in size and colour, so they are easily picked. (e) Partly right. For Heap P she is wrong: 8,000 pebbles take 13 hours 20 minutes by hand against about 3 hours of sieving, and they are far too many to be 'few'. For Heap Q she is right: 60 large stones take 6 minutes by hand, far quicker than 3 hours of sieving.
s: Part (a): holes between 1 mm and 10 mm
Part (b): few particles that are easily picked
Part (c): 8,000 pebbles, 13 h 20 min; 60 stones, 6 min
Part (d): handpicking for the few pebbles left
Part (e): wrong for P (13 h 20 min against 3 h), right for Q (6 min against 3 h)

questions.q:
A Class 6 group tested two kitchen sieves with 500 g of a mixture of semolina (sooji, grains about 0.5 mm) and broken cashew bits. The mixture held 420 g of sooji and 80 g of cashew: 50 g of small bits about 2 mm across and 30 g of large bits about 5 mm across. Sieve X (holes about 1 mm) gave 420 g below and 80 g on top. Sieve Y (holes about 6 mm) gave 500 g below and nothing on top.
(a) Explain why sieve Y separated nothing.
(b) Explain why sieve X held back both sizes of cashew bit.
(c) A sweet shop finds cashew bits bigger than 3 mm too large for its laddoos. What percentage of the cashew is too large?
(d) The shop wants to remove only the too-large bits and keep the small bits with the sooji. Should it use X, Y or a new sieve? Justify, giving a suitable hole size.
questions.a: (a) Its 6 mm holes are larger than the sooji and both sizes of cashew bit, so everything passes. (b) Its 1 mm holes are larger than the 0.5 mm sooji grains but smaller than the 2 mm and 5 mm bits, so all the cashew stays on top. (c) 30 / 80 = 37.5%. (d) A new sieve with holes between 2 mm and 5 mm, about 3 mm: the 5 mm bits stay on top while the 2 mm bits and the sooji pass through together. X would also take out the 50 g of small bits, and Y removes nothing.
s: Part (a): holes bigger than every component
Part (b): holes between sooji and the smallest cashew bits
Part (d): a new sieve of about 3 mm (between 2 and 5 mm), with X and Y rejected

questions.q: After a long football match on a hot day, Arif's navy-blue T-shirt is soaked with sweat, which has some salt dissolved in it. In the evening, when the shirt is dry, it has white patches. What best explains the patches?
questions.a: The water of the sweat evaporated, leaving its dissolved salt on the cloth
o: The water of the sweat evaporated, leaving its dissolved salt on the cloth
The salt of the sweat evaporated, leaving white water marks on the cloth
The sun's heat bleached the blue dye wherever the shirt was dry
The cloth worked as a sieve and held back the larger drops of the sweat

questions.q:
In one salt pan, each litre of seawater leaves 35 g of white solid once the water has evaporated completely.
(a) What mass of solid, in kilograms, will 200 litres of this seawater leave?
(b) A worker drains the pan when only half of the water has evaporated. Will she collect the full amount from (a)? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 200 x 35 = 7,000 g = 7 kg. (b) No, she will collect far less. The salts that are still dissolved in the water she drains away leave with that water; only when the water evaporates completely is all of the dissolved solid left behind.
s: Part (a): 7 kg
Part (b): no; the salt still dissolved in the drained water is lost

questions.q:
Match each mixture in Column I with the method best suited to separate it in Column II.
Column I
1. Common salt fully dissolved in a cup of water
2. Fine clay stirred into a jug of water
3. Iron filings mixed with dry sand
4. Bits of bran in wheat flour
Column II
a. Magnetic separation
b. Evaporation
c. Sieving
d. Filtration

Statement 1: To obtain salt, seawater is stored in deep tanks shaded from the Sun.
Statement 2: Evaporation is the process in which a liquid changes into its vapour.
Statement 3: The solid left behind when seawater dries up in the pits is pure common salt that needs no further treatment.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Meera claims, 'Heating salt solution in a china dish does the same job as the Sun does in the salt pans, only faster: in both cases the water leaves as vapour and the salt is left behind.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. In the salt pans, sunlight and air make the water evaporate over a few days; in the china dish, the flame makes the water boil away in minutes. In both, the water changes into vapour and the dissolved salt stays behind.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
Both are evaporation: water changes into vapour
Both leave the dissolved salt; heating is only quicker

questions.q: Two salt pits on the Gujarat coast each hold 6,000 litres of the same seawater. Pit A has a floor of 30 square metres and is 0.2 m deep; Pit B has a floor of 10 square metres and is 0.6 m deep. Both are in open sunlight. Which pit will give its solid first, and why?
questions.a: Pit A, as its water lies in a shallow layer widely open to sun and air
o: Pit A, as its water lies in a shallow layer widely open to sun and air
Pit B, as its deeper water soaks up much more heat from the Sun each day
Both at once, as they hold exactly the same volume of seawater
Pit B, as its small floor lets the sunlight heat each square metre more strongly

questions.q:
A salt pan beside Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is filled with 20,000 litres of lake water containing 60 g of dissolved salts per litre. The family fills it in April. A trader offers Rs 3 per kg for the dry solid as it is. If the family purifies it first, 25% of the mass is lost as impurities, purifying costs Rs 0.70 for every kilogram of the dry solid put through the purifying (all of it goes in) and takes 4 extra days, and the common salt then sells for Rs 5 per kg.
(a) What mass of solid will the pan give when it dries up?
(b) Give a reason, from how salt is obtained, why the family fills the pan in April and not in the rainy season.
(c) Explain why the dry solid has to be purified before it can be sold as common salt.
(d) Should the family sell the solid as it is or purify it first? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 20,000 x 60 g = 1,200,000 g = 1,200 kg. (b) The water must be exposed to strong sunlight and air so that it evaporates completely in a few days; in the rainy season there is little sun and rain keeps adding water. (c) The lake water has several salts and other substances dissolved in it, so the dry solid is a mixture; common salt is obtained from it by further purification. (d) Selling as it is: 1,200 x 3 = Rs 3,600 at once. Purifying: 900 kg x Rs 5 = Rs 4,500, minus 1,200 x 0.70 = Rs 840 (all 1,200 kg of dry solid goes through the purifying), leaves Rs 3,660, only Rs 60 more after 4 extra days of work. Selling as it is is the better plan; purifying makes sense only if Rs 60 matters more than 4 days.
s: Part (a): 1,200 kg
Part (b): strong sun and air needed for complete evaporation
Part (c): the solid is a mixture of several salts and other substances
Part (d): Rs 3,600 against Rs 3,660, a choice weighing Rs 60 against 4 days

questions.q:
Clear, colourless water from a village hand pump is left in a steel tumbler on a sunny window until it dries. A thin white layer is left on the bottom.
(a) Explain how the white layer formed.
(b) What does this show about water that looks perfectly clear?
questions.a: (a) The water changed into vapour and left, but the substances dissolved in it do not evaporate, so they were left behind as a white solid. (b) Clear water can still have solids dissolved in it; looking clear does not mean it has nothing dissolved in it.
s: Part (a): water evaporated, dissolved solid left behind
Part (b): clear water can still contain dissolved substances

questions.q: A 250 mL glass of salt solution contains 40 g of salt in every litre. When all of its water has evaporated, the mass of salt left behind is ___ g.

A salt farmer near the Rann of Kutch fills a pit 10 m long and 5 m wide with seawater to a depth of 0.1 m. One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres, and each litre of this seawater leaves 35 g of solid when it dries.
(a) How many litres of seawater does the pit hold, and what mass of solid, in kilograms, is left when all the water has evaporated?
(b) Explain why the farmer spreads the water 0.1 m deep over a wide floor instead of storing it in a deep, narrow tank.
(c) Explain why this solid cannot be packed as common salt straight away.
(d) After purification, 80% of the solid is common salt. At Rs 12 per kg, what is the common salt worth?
(e) A visitor suggests covering the pit with a plastic sheet to keep the dust out. Explain what this would do to the salt making.
questions.a: (a) 10 x 5 x 0.1 = 5 cubic metres = 5,000 litres; 5,000 x 35 = 175,000 g = 175 kg. (b) Salt is obtained by keeping seawater in shallow pits exposed to sunlight and air: a thin, wide layer has much more of its water open to the sun and air, so it evaporates completely in a few days; a deep, narrow tank would take far longer. (c) Seawater has several salts and other substances dissolved in it, so the solid left is a mixture; common salt is obtained from it by further purification. (d) 80% of 175 = 140 kg; 140 x 12 = Rs 1,680. (e) The sheet would cut the water off from the air, and the vapour could not escape, so the water would hardly evaporate and the solid would not be left in a few days. The pit must stay open to sunlight and air.
s: Part (a): 5,000 litres and 175 kg
Part (b): shallow, wide layer exposed to sunlight and air evaporates fast
Part (c): the solid is a mixture that needs purification
Part (d): 140 kg, worth Rs 1,680
Part (e): covering blocks air, so the water does not evaporate

questions.q: Riya paints a pattern on black chart paper with a salt solution and lets it dry in the sun. The white pattern is faint. What should she change to get a whiter, thicker pattern next time?
questions.a: Dissolve more salt in the same amount of water before painting
o: Dissolve more salt in the same amount of water before painting
Dry the paper in the shade so that less of the salt evaporates
Add more water to the solution so more salt is left behind
Dry it under a fan so the air blows the salt into the paper

questions.q:
Two china dishes hold equal amounts of the same salt solution. Dish P is heated over a spirit lamp on wire gauze; dish Q is left on a sunny windowsill.
(a) What will be left in each dish once it is dry?
(b) Give one advantage of each way of drying.
questions.a: (a) Salt in both dishes; the water has evaporated from both. (b) Heating (P) is much faster; the windowsill (Q) needs no flame or fuel and is safer.
s: Part (a): salt left in both dishes
Part (b): P faster, Q needs no flame or fuel

questions.q: Sunil leaves a bowl of salt solution open in the sun and hopes to collect both the salt and the water from it. Show why this cannot give him back the water.
questions.a: In the open bowl the water changes into vapour (evaporation) and goes into the air. Nothing collects the vapour, so the water is lost. Only the salt, which does not evaporate, is left in the bowl, so the method gives back the salt but not the water.
s: Water changes into vapour in the open bowl
The vapour escapes into the air and is not collected
Only the salt remains, so only one part is recovered

questions.q: In which of these is the solid left behind NOT the result of evaporation?
questions.a: The clay left at the bottom of a bucket of muddy water after a night
o: The clay left at the bottom of a bucket of muddy water after a night
The white crust left in a pan after salty water has boiled dry
The white patches left on a dark shirt after sweat has dried
The salt crust left on seaside rocks after the pools left by the tide dry up

questions.q: True or False? Sana boils 100 mL of a salt solution dry in a china dish and 4 g of salt is left. Her friend says, 'Salt does not evaporate, so the salt stays the same: if I boil 250 mL of the same solution dry, I will also get 4 g.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. It is true that only the water evaporates and all the dissolved salt is left behind, but 250 mL of the same solution holds more salt: 4 g in 100 mL means 2.5 x 4 = 10 g in 250 mL, so 10 g of salt is left in the dish.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: all the dissolved salt stays, and 250 mL holds 10 g, not 4 g

questions.q:
A Class 6 group made 50 mL of salt solution containing 5 g of salt and split it into three equal parts. Part 1 was spread on black paper on a sunny windowsill and was dry in 40 minutes. Part 2 was heated in a china dish over a spirit lamp and was dry in 12 minutes. Part 3 was kept in a covered bowl in a dark cupboard and was still wet after 2 days.
(a) About how much salt should be left from Part 2 when it is dry?
(b) Explain why Part 3 was still wet.
(c) How many minutes faster was heating than the windowsill?
(d) The teacher has one 45-minute period to show the salt being got back, and on many days clouds cover the sun by mid-morning. A hot china dish must be left about 10 minutes to cool before anyone touches the salt. Which way should she use? Justify with the times and the safety step.
questions.a: (a) Each part holds 5 / 3, about 1.7 g of salt, so about 1.7 g is left. (b) It had no sunlight and was covered from the air, so the water could hardly evaporate. (c) 40 - 12 = 28 minutes faster. (d) A real choice between the two ways that can fit. Heating: 12 minutes to dry plus about 10 to cool = about 22 minutes, well inside 45, and it does not depend on the weather, but it needs a flame and care with the hot dish. Windowsill: 40 minutes of the 45 and no flame, but it leaves only 5 minutes to spare and fails if a cloud hides the sun. The covered bowl cannot work at all. A full-mark answer chooses heating or the windowsill using 22 against 40 minutes and names the safety step for heating (careful heating, letting the dish cool).
s: Part (a): about 1.7 g
Part (b): no sunlight and no open air, so little evaporation
Part (c): 28 minutes
Part (d): a choice using about 22 (12 + 10) against 40 of the 45 minutes, the weather and the safety of the flame

questions.q: A class has finished four separations. For which one is evaporation the right next step?
questions.a: Getting salt from the clear liquid filtered out of salty, sandy water
o: Getting salt from the clear liquid filtered out of salty, sandy water
Getting sand back from a bucket in which it has settled under clear water
Getting chalk from the chalky water poured into a filter-paper cone
Getting a layer of oil off the top of a bowl of water left to stand

questions.q: Explain why a sieve cannot take the salt out of seawater, while evaporation can.
questions.a: The salt is dissolved in the water, so there are no separate solid particles for a sieve to hold back. Evaporation removes the water as vapour, so the dissolved salt is left behind as a solid.
s: Sieve fails: the salt is dissolved, with no separate particles to catch
Evaporation works: water leaves as vapour, the dissolved solid remains

questions.q:
Three liquids are each boiled dry in a china dish. For each one, say whether boiling it dry alone gives a pure solid, and give the reason.
P: Common salt fully dissolved in water that leaves nothing behind when it is boiled dry on its own.
Q: Seawater.
R: Salty water that also has sand in it.
questions.a: P: Yes. Only common salt is dissolved, and the water itself leaves nothing, so pure salt is left when the water evaporates. Q: No. Seawater has several salts and other substances dissolved in it, so a mixture is left, which needs further purification to give common salt. R: No. The sand does not evaporate either, so it is left mixed with the salt; the sand must be removed first, for example by filtration.
s: P: yes, only common salt is dissolved, so pure salt is left
Q: no, seawater leaves a mixture needing purification
R: no, sand stays mixed with the salt unless filtered out first

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Seawater is kept in shallow pits open to sunlight and air to obtain salt.
Reason (R): The solid mixture left after the water evaporates is purified further to obtain common salt.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A class pours 300 mL of the same salt solution, holding 20 g of salt in every litre, into three containers and keeps them side by side in the sun: a wide plate, a cup and a narrow-necked bottle. After one day the plate has lost 180 mL of water, the cup 60 mL and the bottle 10 mL.
(a) How much salt does each container hold at the start?
(b) Explain why the plate lost the most water, linking your answer to how salt pits are made.
(c) If each keeps losing water at the same rate every day, during which day will the plate be dry, and how many days will the cup take?
(d) At the end of day 1, how much salt is in the plate, and why can no solid salt be seen in it yet?
(e) Riya says, 'The bottle will give the most salt in the end, because it lost the least water.' Judge her claim.
questions.a: (a) 0.3 L x 20 g = 6 g in each. (b) The plate spreads the water in a thin, wide layer with the most surface open to the sun and air, so it evaporates fastest; this is why seawater is kept in shallow pits exposed to sunlight and air. (c) The plate: 180 mL on day 1 leaves 120 mL, which is less than one more day's 180 mL, so it is dry during day 2 (300 / 180 = about 1.7 days). The cup: 300 / 60 = 5 days. (d) All 6 g; the salt is still dissolved in the 120 mL of water left, and it is left behind as a solid only when the water has evaporated completely. (e) Wrong. Salt does not evaporate, so every container ends with the same 6 g once it is dry. Losing the least water only means the bottle is slowest: 300 / 10 = 30 days.
s: Part (a): 6 g each
Part (b): widest surface open to sun and air, as in shallow salt pits
Part (c): plate dry during day 2; cup 5 days
Part (d): 6 g still dissolved in 120 mL; solid appears only when all water has gone
Part (e): claim wrong, all give 6 g; the bottle only takes longest (30 days)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Decantation removes even the finest mud particles from muddy water.
Reason (R): In decantation, the liquid on top is removed by tilting the vessel, leaving the settled solid behind.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Ishaan says, 'A filter removes every solid from every liquid. If I pour seawater through filter paper, the water that comes through will have nothing left in it.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No, he is wrong. Filtration separates insoluble solid components from a liquid: the filter holds back particles too big to pass its pores. The salts in seawater are dissolved, so they pass through the filter paper with the water, and the filtrate is still salty. Boiling the filtrate dry would leave the salts behind; only evaporation can get a dissolved solid back.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Filtration holds back only insoluble particles bigger than the pores
Dissolved salts pass through with the water; evaporation is needed to get them back

questions.q: Two jugs of the same muddy pond water are left to stand. Jug P is poured off after 5 minutes; jug Q is left undisturbed for an hour and then poured off just as gently. Kavi says, 'Both pours will give equally muddy water, because decantation never gets all the mud out anyway.' Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Q's water will be clearer, because more mud has settled in an hour, though a little mud may still pass and filtering would be needed to clear it fully
o: Q's water will be clearer, because more mud has settled in an hour, though a little mud may still pass and filtering would be needed to clear it fully
P's water will be clearer, because mud that has settled for an hour gets stirred up more easily while pouring
Kavi is right: since decantation never removes all the mud, the waiting time makes no difference
Both jugs will give perfectly clear water, because decantation removes every insoluble solid once it settles

questions.q:
A filter paper weighs 2 g when dry. Chalky water is poured through it, and once the paper has dried again it weighs 14 g. The filtrate is then boiled dry in a china dish and leaves nothing behind.
(a) What is the residue, and what is its mass?
(b) What does the empty china dish tell you about the chalk?
questions.a: (a) The residue is the chalk held back on the paper: 14 - 2 = 12 g. (b) None of the chalk was dissolved in the water: it is insoluble, so all of it was held back by the filter and nothing was left in the filtrate.
s: Part (a): chalk, 12 g
Part (b): chalk is insoluble, none passed into the filtrate

questions.q:
Match each everyday situation in Column I with the process it shows in Column II.
Column I
1. Muddy water left in a bucket overnight, with the mud collecting at the bottom
2. Water poured off soaked rice by gently tilting the pot
3. Chalky water passed through a fine cotton cloth
4. A plate of salt solution left in the sun until dry
Column II
a. Filtration
b. Evaporation
c. Sedimentation
d. Decantation

(a) Describe one situation in which decantation alone is good enough to separate a solid from a liquid.
(b) Describe one situation in which filtration is needed instead. Give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) Washing rice or pulses: the dirty water is poured off; a few particles left behind do not matter. (b) Getting clear water from muddy pond water: very fine mud does not all settle, and decantation leaves some behind, so a filter with fine pores is needed.
s: Part (a): a situation where some leftover particles do not matter, with reason
Part (b): a situation needing removal of fine particles, with reason

questions.q: Rehana washes a pot of rice before cooking: she adds water, swirls it, waits a few seconds and gently tilts the pot to pour the cloudy water away. Which statement describes what is happening?
questions.a: The rice settles and the dusty water is poured off by decantation
o: The rice settles and the dusty water is poured off by decantation
The dust settles under the rice and is left behind in the pot with it
The rice works like a filter paper and holds back all of the dust
The cloudy water evaporates as it is poured away, leaving the dust

questions.q:
Valli collects pond water that has leaves, sand and fine mud in it. Design a low-cost way to make it clear, using a cut plastic bottle, cotton, clean sand, charcoal pieces, a cloth and a bucket.
(a) What should she do with the water before filtering, and why?
(b) How should she pour the water off the settled solids?
(c) Describe the layers she should place in the bottle and their order.
(d) Explain why more than one kind of filter material is used.
(e) How can she tell whether her filter worked?
questions.a: (a) Let the water stand undisturbed so that the heavier sand and mud settle at the bottom (sedimentation); this keeps most of the solid out of the filter. (b) Tilt the bucket gently and pour off the top water (decantation), leaving the settled solids behind. (c) Any sensible order is accepted if the coarse material meets the water first and the finest last; for example, from the top where the water is poured in: cloth (catches leaves), clean sand, charcoal pieces, and a cotton plug in the neck. (d) The choice of filter depends on the size of the particles to be removed: the cloth holds back larger bits, while sand, charcoal and cotton catch finer particles. (e) Compare the water collected (the filtrate) with the pond water: it should be clearer, with the solids left as residue in the layers. (Any fair before-and-after comparison is accepted.)
s: Part (a): sedimentation first, with reason
Part (b): decantation by tilting
Part (c): any sensible order with coarse material first, finest last
Part (d): different materials for different particle sizes
Part (e): compare clearness of filtrate, residue left behind

questions.q: Pond water holds three kinds of solid: sand grains about 0.5 mm, leaf bits about 5 mm and silt about 0.02 mm across. It is poured through a cloth whose pores are about 0.05 mm wide. The kind of solid that comes through into the filtrate is the ___.
questions.a: silt

questions.q: Kiran claims, 'If muddy water is left standing overnight and then poured off carefully, it becomes just as clear as water that has been through filter paper.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Standing overnight lets the heavier mud settle (sedimentation), and careful pouring is decantation, but decantation does not completely separate all the particles: some fine mud is carried along. Filter paper, with its very fine pores, holds back even these fine particles, so the filtered water is clearer.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Sedimentation plus decantation leaves some fine particles in the water
Filter paper's fine pores remove these, so filtered water is clearer

questions.q: Valli pours muddy pond water through a folded cotton cloth. The water that comes through is clearer but still slightly muddy. What should she do next to get clear water?
questions.a: Pass it through filter paper, whose pores are much finer than cloth's
o: Pass it through filter paper, whose pores are much finer than cloth's
Pass it through a flour sieve, whose holes are larger than the gaps in cloth
Pour it through the same cloth again, but much faster this time round
Boil it all away in a china dish so that only the clean water is left

questions.q: True or False? Muddy water poured through a tea strainer will still look muddy, even though the same strainer holds back all the leaves from a cup of tea. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The choice of filter depends on the size of the particles to be removed. The strainer's holes are smaller than tea leaves but much larger than mud particles, so the mud passes through with the water; a cloth or a filter paper with finer pores is needed.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: mud particles are far smaller than the strainer's holes; the filter must suit the particle size

questions.q:
A roadside tea stall in Puducherry makes tea in batches of 6 litres and serves it in 150 mL cups. Today its strainer is broken. The owner lets each pan stand for a few minutes and then tilts it gently to pour. From experience, about 1 cup in every 8 poured this way has a few tea leaves in it, and he gives Rs 4 back on each such cup. Pouring a batch through a clean muslin cloth instead takes 6 extra minutes; in the morning rush he reckons each minute of waiting loses him Rs 4 of sales, while in the quiet afternoon waiting costs him nothing.
(a) What process makes the leaves collect at the bottom of the pan while it stands?
(b) How many cups does one batch fill?
(c) About how many cups in a batch will have tea leaves in them?
(d) For each batch, should he keep decanting or pour through the muslin cloth, in the morning rush and in the afternoon? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Sedimentation: the heavier, insoluble tea leaves settle at the bottom. (b) 6,000 / 150 = 40 cups. (c) 40 / 8 = 5 cups. (d) Decanting costs 5 x Rs 4 = Rs 20 a batch, because decantation lets some leaves through; pouring through muslin is filtration, which catches the leaves, but costs 6 x Rs 4 = Rs 24 of lost sales in the rush and nothing in the afternoon. So: decant in the morning rush (Rs 20 against Rs 24) and filter through muslin in the afternoon (Rs 0 against Rs 20). An answer that filters in the rush too, arguing that leaves in cups lose customers beyond the Rs 4, is accepted if it uses the numbers.
s: Part (a): sedimentation
Part (b): 40 cups
Part (c): about 5 cups
Part (d): Rs 20 against Rs 24 in the rush and Rs 20 against Rs 0 in the afternoon, with a choice for each

questions.q:
Statement 1: Sedimentation is the settling of a heavier insoluble component at the bottom of a liquid.
Statement 2: The choice of a filter depends on the size of the particles to be removed.
Statement 3: Decantation is also used when washing and cleaning rice and pulses.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
Valli pours muddy water through a single layer of cotton cloth and the water that comes through is still cloudy. She then folds the cloth into four layers and filters the cloudy water again.
(a) Will the water now be clearer, more cloudy, or the same?
(b) Give a reason, using what makes cloth work as a filter.
questions.a: (a) Clearer. (b) Cloth filters through the very small pores between its woven threads. With four layers, the water has to pass through many layers of threads, so more of the fine mud particles that slipped through one layer are held back. (An answer saying the pores stay the same size but the extra layers give the mud more chances to be caught is also correct.)
s: Part (a): clearer
Part (b): more layers of threads and pores hold back more fine particles

questions.q: Write a short kitchen situation in which sedimentation followed by decantation is used. Name what settles, what is poured off, and one reason why the result might not be perfectly clean.
questions.a: Example: Amma soaks rajma in water and stirs it; small bits of soil and grit settle at the bottom of the pot (sedimentation). She tilts the pot and pours the dirty water off the beans (decantation). A little grit may still be carried with the beans, because decantation does not separate everything completely.
s: A kitchen situation with something settling at the bottom
Liquid poured off by tilting, named as decantation
Limitation: decantation is not complete

questions.q: A village group is building a low-cost water filter in a cut plastic bottle. Which layer would NOT work as a filter, and why?
questions.a: Common salt, as it dissolves in the water instead of holding solids back
o: Common salt, as it dissolves in the water instead of holding solids back
Cotton, as its fibres leave only tiny gaps for the water to pass through
Charcoal, as its pieces trap fine particles in the small gaps between them
Sand, as the gaps between its grains are smaller than most bits of mud

questions.q:
Some mustard oil has been spilt into a bowl of 2 litres of water and, after a few minutes, forms a separate layer on top: 300 mL of oil. Rafiq tilts the bowl and pours the top layer into a jug, stopping as soon as water starts to come; the jug holds 280 mL, all oil.
(a) Name the method, and explain why the oil, not the water, is poured off.
(b) How much oil is still in the bowl, and why did Rafiq stop before all of it was out?
questions.a: (a) Decantation: the oil does not mix with water and forms a separate layer on top, so tilting the bowl pours the top layer off first. (b) 300 - 280 = 20 mL. Near the end the thin oil layer and the water come out together, so pouring on would carry water into the jug; decantation does not separate the two completely.
s: Part (a): decantation; the oil is the separate top layer
Part (b): 20 mL left; pouring further brings water too, decantation is incomplete

questions.q: Compare a fishing net with a filter paper used for muddy water. Give one way they are alike and two ways they are different.
questions.a: Alike: both let the liquid (water) pass through openings while holding back solids that are bigger than the openings. Different: (1) the net's mesh is large, while the filter paper's pores are very fine; (2) the net holds back fish and big rubbish such as plastic bags and bottles, while the filter paper holds back tiny mud particles.
s: Likeness: liquid passes, larger solids are held back
Difference in size of openings
Difference in what is held back

questions.q:
A class tested four ways of cleaning 500 mL samples of the same muddy water.
Method 1: stood 10 minutes, then poured off: 400 mL, cloudy.
Method 2: stood 2 hours, then poured off: 420 mL, slightly cloudy.
Method 3: poured through cotton cloth: 450 mL, slightly cloudy.
Method 4: poured through filter paper: 440 mL, clear.
(a) Why was the water from Method 2 clearer than from Method 1?
(b) Why could neither Method 1 nor Method 2 give all 500 mL back?
(c) Which method gave the most water, and how much more than Method 1?
(d) Why did Method 4 give the clearest water?
(e) Suggest a combination of methods that would give clear water with less mud reaching the filter. Justify.
questions.a: (a) In 2 hours more of the heavier mud settled at the bottom (more sedimentation), so less was carried over when pouring. (b) Some water has to be left behind with the settled mud, since tipping it all out would carry the mud too; decantation does not separate completely. (c) Method 3 (cloth): 450 mL, which is 50 mL more than Method 1. (d) Filter paper has very fine pores that hold back even small mud particles. (e) Let the water stand for 2 hours, pour it off carefully, then pass it through filter paper: most mud stays at the bottom of the vessel, and the paper removes the fine particles left, giving clear water.
s: Part (a): longer standing, more sedimentation
Part (b): water must be left with the sediment, decantation incomplete
Part (c): Method 3, 50 mL more
Part (d): fine pores of filter paper
Part (e): sedimentation and decantation, then filter paper, justified

questions.q:
A school garden club collects 20 litres of pond water in a bucket. It has floating dry leaves, sand and fine clay that make it brown. They have two filters: a filter-paper set-up that passes 1 litre in about 6.5 minutes, and a cotton cloth folded in four that passes 1 litre in about 3 minutes.
(a) What will happen to the sand if the bucket is left undisturbed for an hour, and what is this called?
(b) After an hour they pour off 17 litres, leaving the rest with the sediment. What percentage of the water is left behind, and why can they not pour it all off?
(c) Which of the two filters is more likely to remove the fine clay that makes the water brown? Explain.
(d) They need 10 litres of water for their seedlings within one hour, and the gardener prefers clear water. Which filter should they use? Justify with numbers and your answer to (c).
questions.a: (a) The heavier sand settles at the bottom; this is sedimentation. (b) 20 - 17 = 3 litres, 3 / 20 = 15%; tipping out the last of the water would carry the settled solids with it, as decantation cannot separate completely. (c) The filter paper, because its pores are much finer than the gaps in cloth, so it holds back the fine clay that passes through cloth. (d) A real trade-off: the filter paper takes 10 x 6.5 = 65 minutes, 5 minutes more than the hour, but gives clear water; the cloth takes 10 x 3 = 30 minutes but leaves the water slightly brown. A full-mark answer chooses one, using 65 against 30 minutes and the clay left by cloth.
s: Part (a): sand settles, sedimentation
Part (b): 15%, with the reason decantation cannot be complete
Part (c): filter paper, finer pores catch fine clay
Part (d): a choice using 65 against 30 minutes and clearness

questions.q:
Statement 1: In churning, butter floats to the top because it is lighter.
Statement 2: Scrap iron pulled out of waste by magnets on cranes can be recycled and reused.
Statement 3: When the carpenter moved a magnet through the sawdust, both the iron nails and the sawdust stuck to it.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
The carpenter first started picking the dropped nails out of the sawdust by hand.
(a) Why was handpicking a slow choice here?
(b) Name the better method and say why it works.
questions.a: (a) The nails were many and small and hidden in the sawdust, so they were not few and easily picked. (b) Magnetic separation: iron nails are attracted to a magnet and sawdust is not, so moving a magnet through the sawdust pulls out all the nails.
s: Part (a): nails were many and hidden, not few and easily picked
Part (b): magnetic separation, iron attracted and sawdust not

questions.q: A carpenter in Shillong knocks a box of about 200 small iron nails into a heap of sawdust. Which method will get the nails back fastest?
questions.a: Moving a magnet through the sawdust, as only the iron nails are attracted
o: Moving a magnet through the sawdust, as only the iron nails are attracted
Winnowing the heap in a breeze, as the iron nails are lighter than sawdust
Stirring the heap in water so the sawdust dissolves, then filtering
Picking out the nails one by one, as handpicking is quickest for many nails

questions.q:
Kamla tests how long to churn curd. She churns 4 litres of curd with a mathni and weighs the butter collected after different times: 5 minutes, 60 g; 10 minutes, 120 g; 15 minutes, 150 g; 20 minutes, 155 g; 25 minutes, 155 g.
(a) Why does the butter collect at the top of the pot, where she can lift it off?
(b) How much butter did she get for each litre of curd after 20 minutes?
(c) How much extra butter did the last 10 minutes of churning give, compared with stopping at 15 minutes? What does this suggest about the curd by then?
(d) What percentage of the final 155 g had she collected by 15 minutes? Give the answer to one decimal place.
(e) Kamla churns every morning and is short of time. Recommend a churning time and justify it with the data. Say what she should do with the liquid left in the pot.
questions.a: (a) Butter is lighter, so it floats at the top while the buttermilk is left behind. (b) 155 / 4 = 38.75 g per litre. (c) 155 - 150 = 5 g; almost all the butter had already separated by 15 minutes, so further churning gives very little. (d) 150 / 155 = 96.8%. (e) About 15 minutes: it gives 96.8% of the butter, and the next 10 minutes add only 5 g. (A choice of 20 minutes is accepted if it argues that the last 5 g matter.) The liquid left is buttermilk, a useful product (chhach) to drink, so churning gives two useful components.
s: Part (a): butter is lighter and floats
Part (b): 38.75 g per litre
Part (c): 5 g extra; nearly all butter already separated
Part (e): about 15 minutes justified with the data; buttermilk kept as a useful product

questions.q: In a classroom fishing game, cardboard fish each have a small iron clip attached, and the fishing rod has a magnet tied to its thread. Why can the rod lift the fish?
questions.a: The iron clip is attracted to the magnet and carries the cardboard fish with it
o: The iron clip is attracted to the magnet and carries the cardboard fish with it
Cardboard is a magnetic substance, so the fish would be lifted even without a clip
The thread is sticky, and the magnet only adds weight so the thread sinks
Any light object is pulled up by a magnet, whether or not it has iron in it

questions.q: A dairy gets 90 g of butter from every 2 litres of curd it churns. To fill an order for 4.5 kg of butter, it must churn ___ litres of curd.

Raju has lost an aluminium ring in a heap of sawdust. In class he saw a magnet tested on a heap holding iron nails and aluminium foil strips: the nails jumped to the magnet and the foil did not move. Still he says, 'A magnet can pull any metal object out of sawdust, so a strong magnet will find my ring.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No, he is wrong. Magnetic separation works only for substances that are attracted to a magnet, such as iron. The class test showed that aluminium foil is not attracted (it did not move while the iron nails did), so an aluminium ring will not be pulled out either and will stay in the sawdust; a magnet picks out iron objects, not every metal. He will have to sieve or handpick the ring out instead.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Only magnetic substances such as iron are attracted
Aluminium is not attracted (as the foil showed), so the ring stays; another method is needed

questions.q:
A small dairy churns curd every morning. On average, every litre of curd gives 40 g of butter. A wedding order needs 3 kg of butter by 2 pm, and churning can begin at 6 am. A worker with a hand mathni churns 10 litres an hour at no extra cost; the dairy could instead hire an electric churner for Rs 200 for the day, which handles 40 litres an hour and uses electricity costing Rs 16 an hour.
(a) Which part of the churned curd is collected for the order, and why does it come to the top?
(b) How many litres of curd are needed for 3 kg of butter?
(c) How long would the hand mathni take for this amount?
(d) Should the dairy churn by hand or hire the electric churner? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) The butter, because it is lighter and floats while the buttermilk is left behind. (b) 3,000 / 40 = 75 litres. (c) 75 / 10 = 7.5 hours. (d) A real trade-off. By hand: 7.5 hours from 6 am ends at 1:30 pm, only 30 minutes before the order is due, but costs nothing extra. Electric: 75 / 40 = 1.875 hours (about 1 hour 53 minutes), done before 8 am, but costs Rs 200 + 1.875 x 16 = Rs 230. A full-mark answer chooses one, weighing Rs 230 against a 30-minute safety margin (for example: churn by hand and save Rs 230, or pay Rs 230 so that a delay cannot spoil the order).
s: Part (a): butter, lighter so it floats
Part (b): 75 litres
Part (c): 7.5 hours
Part (d): a choice weighing Rs 230 (200 + 30) against finishing at 1:30 pm with 30 minutes to spare

questions.q: At a dhaba, the owner churns curd in an electric mixer instead of with a big mathni. What happens to the butter?
questions.a: It still gathers at the top, because it is lighter than the buttermilk
o: It still gathers at the top, because it is lighter than the buttermilk
None forms, because only a wooden mathni can separate butter from curd
It sinks to the bottom, because the fast blades push it downwards
It mixes into one liquid with the buttermilk, so nothing separates

questions.q:
By mistake, Bua tips some iron filings, each about the same size as a grain of sooji, into a bag of sooji (semolina).
(a) Name a method that will separate them, and say why it works.
(b) Explain why sieving is a poor choice here, even though she has a sieve.
questions.a: (a) Magnetic separation: the iron filings are attracted to a magnet and the sooji is not, so moving a magnet through the sooji pulls the filings out. (b) Sieving needs components of different sizes; the filings are about the same size as the sooji grains, so they would pass through (or stay on) the sieve together with the sooji.
s: Part (a): magnet, iron attracted, sooji not
Part (b): same size, so a sieve cannot separate them

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When curd is churned, butter collects at the top.
Reason (R): After the butter is taken out, buttermilk is left behind.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A tailor's tin holds iron pins, a few large plastic buttons and some dried peas, all mixed. Describe how to separate the three, giving the property used at each step.
questions.a: First move a magnet through the tin: the iron pins are attracted and come out (magnetic separation), since buttons and peas are not magnetic. Then pick out the few large plastic buttons by hand, using their different size, colour and shape (handpicking); a sieve whose holes let the peas through but hold back the larger buttons would also work. The dried peas are left.
s: Magnet removes iron pins, as they are magnetic
Buttons removed by handpicking (or a suitable sieve), by size, colour or shape
Peas left as the last component

questions.q: A crane magnet makes three lifts over a 2,500 kg heap of waste holding iron scrap, broken glass and plastic, and the heap then weighs 2,050 kg. Workers sorting the rest by hand later find 30 kg of iron bolts that had been buried deep under the glass. What percentage of the heap's iron did the crane miss?
questions.a: 6.25%, as the heap held 450 + 30 = 480 kg of iron, and glass and plastic are not attracted
o: 6.25%, as the heap held 450 + 30 = 480 kg of iron, and glass and plastic are not attracted
6.67%, because the crane lifted 450 kg of iron and 30 kg is that fraction of what it actually lifted
1.2%, because 30 kg is that fraction of the whole 2,500 kg heap
1.46%, because 30 kg is that fraction of the 2,050 kg of waste left in the heap after the three lifts

questions.q: True or False? In churning, the butter comes to the top only because the mathni pushes it up; if the churning stops and the pot is left to stand, the butter sinks back to the bottom. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The butter comes to the top because it is lighter than the buttermilk, so it floats there and stays on top when the churning stops; it does not sink back.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: butter is lighter, so it floats and stays at the top

questions.q: Valli drags a strong magnet through dry beach sand. It comes out coated with tiny black grains, while the light-brown grains stay behind. What does this show?
questions.a: The black grains have a magnetic substance such as iron; the brown ones do not
o: The black grains have a magnetic substance such as iron; the brown ones do not
Every black object is magnetic, so the magnet picks out dark colours
A magnet attracts the smallest grains in a mixture, whatever they are made of
The black grains are heavier, and a magnet attracts the heaviest grains

questions.q: Dev suggests moving a strong magnet through a pot of churned curd to pull the butter out of the buttermilk. Show why this cannot work, and say what does work.
questions.a: Magnetic separation works only when one component is a magnetic substance, attracted to the magnet. Neither butter nor buttermilk is attracted to a magnet, so the magnet pulls out nothing. Butter is separated by churning, because it is lighter and floats to the top.
s: Magnetic separation needs a magnetic component
Neither butter nor buttermilk is magnetic, so nothing is pulled out
