Churning works, because butter is lighter and floats

questions.q:
A recycling yard receives 5,000 kg of mixed waste every day, of which 12% by mass is scrap iron.
(a) Explain why the crane magnet lifts out a steel almirah from the heap but leaves behind a wooden almirah of the same size.
(b) If scrap iron sells for Rs 25 per kg, how much money does separating the iron bring in each day?
questions.a: (a) Steel contains iron, a magnetic substance, so it is attracted to the magnet; wood is non-magnetic, so it is not attracted, whatever its size. (b) 12% of 5,000 kg = 600 kg; 600 x 25 = Rs 15,000 a day.
s: Part (a): steel (iron) is magnetic, wood is not; size does not matter
Part (b): 600 kg, Rs 15,000

questions.q: For which of these mixtures would moving a magnet through it NOT separate the two parts?
questions.a: Iron filings mixed with small iron nails
o: Iron filings mixed with small iron nails
Iron filings mixed into wheat flour
Steel pins mixed with rice grains
Iron nails mixed with sawdust

questions.q:
Kamla churns curd with a mathni and lifts the butter off the top.
(a) What is left behind in the pot?
(b) Is this separation done to remove a useless part, or to get two useful parts? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Buttermilk. (b) To get two different but useful parts: butter is used in cooking, and buttermilk (chhach) is drunk, so neither is thrown away.
s: Part (a): buttermilk
Part (b): two useful parts, as both butter and buttermilk are used

questions.q: A 500 g mixture of iron filings and sand is 30% iron filings by mass. A magnet moved through it picks up 140 g of filings. The mass of iron filings still left in the sand is ___ g.

In a carpenter's workshop, about 200 iron nails fall into a 15 kg heap of sawdust about twice a week. His small magnet picks up about 25 nails in each 30-second sweep through the heap. Picking nails out by hand takes him about 6 seconds a nail. A larger magnet costing Rs 150 would clear the heap in 2 sweeps. He reckons his working time is worth Rs 1 a minute, and he will stay in this workshop for 26 more weeks.
(a) Why is the sawdust left behind when a magnet is swept through?
(b) How many minutes does the small magnet save on each spill, compared with handpicking all the nails?
(c) How many minutes a week would the larger magnet save compared with the small one, and after how many weeks would it pay for itself?
(d) Should he buy the larger magnet? Justify using (c).
questions.a: (a) Sawdust is not a magnetic substance, so it is not attracted; only the iron nails are. (b) Handpicking: 200 x 6 s = 1,200 s = 20 minutes; small magnet: 200 / 25 = 8 sweeps x 30 s = 4 minutes; it saves 16 minutes. (c) Larger magnet: 2 x 30 s = 1 minute, so 3 minutes saved per spill, 6 minutes (Rs 6) a week; Rs 150 / Rs 6 = 25 weeks to pay for itself. (d) A close call: over his 26 weeks it saves about Rs 156, only Rs 6 more than its price, so it barely pays for itself. A full-mark answer decides either way using the 25 weeks against 26, for example 'not worth it, the gain is tiny' or 'worth it, since it pays back and he can take it with him'.
s: Part (a): sawdust is non-magnetic
Part (b): 16 minutes saved
Part (c): 6 minutes a week, pays back in 25 weeks
Part (d): a judgement using 25 weeks against the 26 weeks left

questions.q:
A recycling yard receives 12,000 kg of mixed waste, of which 18% by mass is scrap iron. Its crane magnet can lift up to 300 kg of iron in one lift.
(a) What mass of scrap iron is in the waste, and what is the least number of lifts needed to remove it all?
(b) In one lift, a plastic bag came up with the iron, wrapped tightly round an iron rod. Explain why, although plastic is not magnetic.
(c) After the iron is out, the heap still holds shredded paper and broken glass. Suggest a method from this chapter to separate them, and the difference between them that it depends on.
(d) If scrap iron sells for Rs 28 per kg, what is the iron worth?
(e) Which of the two purposes of separating substances does this yard serve when it pulls out the iron? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 18% of 12,000 = 2,160 kg; 2,160 / 300 = 7.2, so 8 lifts. (b) The magnet attracts only the iron rod; the bag is fastened to the rod, so it is carried up with it, just as an iron clip carries a cardboard fish up to a magnet. (c) Blowing air across the heap, as in winnowing: the shredded paper is light and is carried away, while the heavier glass falls close by. (Handpicking, if the paper bits are few, is also accepted with its reason.) (d) 2,160 x 28 = Rs 60,480. (e) It obtains a useful component: the scrap iron can be recycled and reused instead of being dumped with the waste.
s: Part (a): 2,160 kg and 8 lifts (7.2 rounded up)
Part (b): only the iron is attracted; the bag is carried because it is attached
Part (c): blowing air (winnowing), light paper carried off, heavier glass stays
Part (d): Rs 60,480
Part (e): getting a useful component, the scrap iron, for recycling

questions.q: A mixture contains dried whole peas, chalk powder and common salt. Outline a stepwise procedure to get each component separately, naming the method used at each step.
questions.a: 1. Remove the peas by sieving (or handpicking), since they are much bigger than the powders. 2. Stir the remaining powder in water: the salt dissolves, the chalk does not; filter, so the chalk stays as residue. 3. Evaporate the filtrate to get the salt back.
s: Peas removed by sieving or handpicking, by size
Water added and chalk filtered out as residue
Filtrate evaporated to recover the salt

questions.q: Before planning how to separate a mixture of salt, black pepper and stones that has been tipped into water, which question decides whether evaporation will be needed?
questions.a: Does any component dissolve in the water?
o: Does any component dissolve in the water?
Is any component bigger than the others?
Are all the components the same colour?
Is any component attracted to a magnet?

questions.q:
A 300 g dry mixture of iron filings, chalk powder and common salt is separated. A magnet removes 60 g. The rest is stirred into water and filtered, and the dried residue weighs 140 g.
(a) Which component is the residue, and where is the third component now?
(b) If nothing is lost, what mass should be left when the filtrate is evaporated?
questions.a: (a) The residue is the chalk, which does not dissolve; the salt has dissolved and is in the filtrate. (b) 300 - 60 - 140 = 100 g of salt.
s: Part (a): chalk as residue, salt dissolved in the filtrate
Part (b): 100 g

questions.q:
Ravi's mother finds that a 2 kg bag of rice (grains about 2 mm thick) has got mixed with 200 g of fine sand (grains about 0.3 mm) and about 40 small iron pins from a broken box. She has a magnet, a sieve with 1 mm holes and a bowl of water.
(a) Which component will the magnet remove, and why do the others stay?
(b) What will the sieve do with the rice and sand? Explain using the hole size.
(c) After sieving, only 1.98 kg of rice is left on the sieve. What mass of rice passed through with the sand, and why could it pass?
(d) Her neighbour says, 'Skip the sieve: just wash the rice in water and pour the water off, the way we wash rice every day.' Will that remove the sand? Judge the plan.
questions.a: (a) The iron pins: iron is a magnetic substance and is attracted, while rice and sand are not. (b) The 1 mm holes are larger than the 0.3 mm sand grains but smaller than the 2 mm rice grains, so the sand passes through and the rice stays on top. (c) 2.00 - 1.98 = 0.02 kg = 20 g; these were broken bits of rice smaller than 1 mm. (d) No. Decantation pours off the water and what floats or stays mixed in it, such as dust; the sand is heavy and settles at the bottom with the rice, so it stays in the pot. Washing is fine for dust, but the sieve is needed for the sand.
s: Part (a): iron pins, the only magnetic component
Part (b): sand passes the 1 mm holes, rice stays
Part (c): 20 g of broken bits smaller than 1 mm
Part (d): plan rejected; heavy sand settles with the rice, so decanting leaves it

questions.q: Valli sorts four jobs into two baskets: 'get two useful parts' and 'remove a part that is not useful'. Which job belongs in the 'get two useful parts' basket?
questions.a: A builder sieves a heap, using the sand for plaster and the gravel left behind for concrete
o: A builder sieves a heap, using the sand for plaster and the gravel left behind for concrete
A builder sieves a heap for plaster and throws away the pebbles left on the sieve
Mami sieves fresh atta and throws away the bran and the small stones that are left on the sieve
Amma pours the cloudy water off a pot of washed rice and then cooks the rice that is left behind

questions.q: Tara says, 'A dry mixture of iron filings, sand and common salt, in which the sand grains and salt grains are the same size, cannot be separated by any single method from this chapter. I will need at least three methods.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. No one method acts on all three: a magnet takes out only the iron filings; since the sand and salt grains are the same size, a sieve cannot part them, so the salt must be dissolved in water and the sand filtered out; and the salt is got back by evaporating the filtrate. That is magnetic separation, filtration and evaporation, three methods.
s: Verdict: the claim is right
Magnet removes only the iron; equal grain sizes rule out sieving, so dissolve and filter out the sand
Evaporation is still needed for the salt, making three methods

questions.q:
Statement 1: A mixture with more than two components generally needs a combination of several methods of separation.
Statement 2: To recover both parts of a sand-salt mixture after adding water, the water is evaporated first and the sand filtered out afterwards.
Statement 3: In a mixture of sand, salt and water, filter paper holds back the salt along with the sand.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Common salt and whole black peppercorns have got mixed in a jar.
(a) Describe two different ways of separating them, each using a different property of the components.
(b) Which of your two ways gives back the salt without any heating or drying? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Way 1: sieve (or handpick) out the peppercorns, which are much bigger and darker than the salt grains: difference in size or colour. Way 2: stir the mixture in water so that the salt dissolves, filter out the peppercorns, and evaporate the filtrate to get the salt: the salt dissolves and the pepper does not. (b) The sieving or handpicking way: the salt is never dissolved, so it stays dry and needs no evaporation.
s: Part (a): one way by size or colour and one by dissolving, filtering and evaporating
Part (b): the dry way, as the salt is never dissolved

questions.q: A dry mixture contains iron filings, sawdust and common salt. Which sequence will separate all three?
questions.a: Magnet, add water, filter out the sawdust, evaporate the filtrate
o: Magnet, add water, filter out the sawdust, evaporate the filtrate
Magnet, add water, evaporate it, then filter out the sawdust
Magnet, pour the dry mix through filter paper, evaporate what passes
Add water, decant off the salt, then use a magnet on the sawdust

questions.q:
A group took 100 g of a sand-salt mixture, stirred it in water, filtered it, and evaporated the filtrate. They got 22 g of salt and, after drying, 74 g of sand.
(a) What total mass did they recover, and what percentage of the mixture was lost?
(b) Explain why the salt went through the filter paper while the sand stayed on it, and why the salt could be got back only by evaporation.
(c) Suggest one place in the procedure where some of the mixture could have been lost.
(d) If the salt had not fully dissolved before filtering, how would the masses of sand and salt recovered change? Explain.
(e) Suggest one change that would make the salt result more reliable.
questions.a: (a) 22 + 74 = 96 g; 100 - 96 = 4 g, which is 4%. (b) Filtration separates insoluble solids from a liquid: the sand does not dissolve and its grains are held back as residue, but the salt is dissolved, so it passes through the pores with the water. Only evaporating the water leaves the dissolved salt behind as a solid. (c) For example, sand left stuck to the filter paper or the beaker, or salt solution left soaked in the wet residue. (d) Undissolved salt would stay on the filter paper with the sand, so the 'sand' mass would be too high and the salt mass too low. (e) Stir longer, until no salt is seen, before filtering (or rinse the residue with a little water so the salt in it reaches the filtrate).
s: Part (a): 96 g and 4%
Part (b): insoluble sand held back, dissolved salt passes; evaporation leaves the salt
Part (c): a sensible place of loss
Part (d): sand mass up, salt mass down, with reason
Part (e): a sensible change such as stirring until fully dissolved

questions.q: Which of these jobs needs two or more methods used one after another, rather than a single method?
questions.a: Getting dry sand and dry salt back from a mixture of equal-sized grains
o: Getting dry sand and dry salt back from a mixture of equal-sized grains
Removing bran from wheat flour before kneading it into dough
Getting butter out of a pot of curd
Removing dropped iron nails from a large heap of sawdust

questions.q: True or False? When Mami sieves the bran out of flour before making puris, and when a mill sieves rava into coarse and fine grades that are both sold, the two separations serve the same purpose. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Mami removes a component that is not useful: the bran has to be taken out before the flour is used. The mill obtains two different but useful components, since both grades are sold. They serve the two different purposes of separation.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: bran removal removes a part not useful; grading rava gives two useful parts

questions.q: A bucket that holds mustard oil, water and sand has been left undisturbed overnight. Plan how to get the oil, the water and the sand separately, in order, and say why the oil is taken off first.
questions.a: 1. While it stands, the heavier sand settles at the bottom (sedimentation) and the oil, which does not mix with water, forms a separate layer on top. 2. Tilt the bucket gently and pour off the oil layer into another container (decantation). The oil comes first because it lies on top and can be poured off without disturbing the rest. 3. Pour the water through a filter paper or cloth: the water passes as filtrate and the sand stays as residue (or decant the water off the settled sand and filter what is left).
s: Sand settles and oil forms a top layer on standing
Oil decanted first, because it is the top layer
Water and sand separated by filtration (or decantation then filtration)

questions.q: A dry mixture of chalk powder and common salt is stirred in water and filtered. The dried residue weighs 30 g, and boiling the filtrate dry leaves 18 g. If nothing was lost, common salt made up ___ % of the mixture.

A beaker holds iron filings and chalk powder stirred into water.
(a) Which method should be used first if no iron filings are to be lost, and why?
(b) Which method then separates the chalk from the water?
questions.a: (a) Magnetic separation: iron is attracted to a magnet while chalk and water are not. Doing it first takes out the filings before they get trapped in the wet chalk on the filter paper, where some would be missed. (b) Filtration: the insoluble chalk stays on the filter paper as residue and the water passes through as filtrate.
s: Part (a): magnet first, iron is magnetic, so no filings get trapped in the chalk residue
Part (b): filtration, chalk as residue

questions.q:
Volunteers at a beach clean-up in Chennai collect 30 kg of beach material. It includes 2 kg of iron bottle caps and 1.5 kg of plastic bits; the rest is sand. All the caps and plastic bits are bigger than the sand grains. A recycler pays Rs 30 per kg for the caps. Plastic left on the beach can be washed into the sea, where it harms fish.
(a) Which method will take out only the bottle caps, and why?
(b) What percentage of the 30 kg of beach material is bottle caps?
(c) Which method will separate the plastic bits from the sand, what must be true of the tool, and how much sand is left once both jobs are done?
(d) There is time for only one of the two jobs today. Which should be done? Justify, using the two purposes of separation and the numbers.
questions.a: (a) Magnetic separation: the iron caps are attracted to a magnet, while sand and plastic are not. (b) 2 / 30 = about 6.7%. (c) Sieving: the holes must be smaller than the plastic bits but larger than the sand grains; 30 - 2 - 1.5 = 26.5 kg of sand is left. (d) A real choice between the two purposes: taking out the caps obtains a useful component worth 2 x 30 = Rs 60; taking out the plastic removes a component that is not useful and harms fish. A full-mark answer names the purpose each job serves and argues for one, using Rs 60 against the harm.
s: Part (a): magnet, iron caps are magnetic
Part (b): about 6.7%
Part (c): sieving, holes between plastic and sand sizes; 26.5 kg of sand
Part (d): a choice linked to the two purposes, using Rs 60 against the harm to fish

questions.q:
A tin holds chana dal with a large amount of puffed rice and a few small stones mixed in.
(a) Which method removes the puffed rice, and why does it work?
(b) Which method removes the stones, and why can the first method not remove them?
questions.a: (a) Winnowing: the puffed rice is light and is carried away by moving air, while the heavier chana dal falls close by. (b) Handpicking: the stones are few and differ in colour and shape. They are heavy, so they fall with the chana dal and moving air cannot carry them away.
s: Part (a): winnowing, light puffed rice carried off
Part (b): handpicking; heavy stones fall with the dal, so winnowing fails

questions.a: Stirring the mixture in water so that the salt dissolves
o: Stirring the mixture in water so that the salt dissolves
Heating the dry mixture in a china dish until it glows
Churning the dry mixture until the salt floats to the top

questions.q: A student's procedure reads: 'Handpick, then use a magnet, then add water and filter, then evaporate the filtrate.' Invent a mixture of four components for which this procedure is exactly right, and say what each step removes.
questions.a: Example: a few large pebbles, iron nails, sand and common salt. Handpicking removes the few pebbles; the magnet removes the iron nails; adding water dissolves the salt and filtering holds back the sand; evaporating the filtrate leaves the salt.
s: Four components that fit the four steps
Handpicking and magnet steps matched to the right components
Filtration for the insoluble part, evaporation for the dissolved part

questions.q:
You are given a bucket containing iron pins, sand, dry chickpeas, common salt and water. Plan how to get each solid component back separately.
(a) Which component can be removed by hand, and why is that easy?
(b) How would you remove the iron pins?
(c) How would you separate the sand from the salty water?
(d) How would you get the salt back?
(e) Explain why the salt must be the last component recovered.
questions.a: (a) The chickpeas, because they are large and easy to see and pick out (a strainer that holds back the chickpeas also works). They can be taken out before or after the pins. (b) Move a magnet through the mixture: the iron pins are attracted, the rest is not. (c) Let the sand settle (sedimentation), decant the salty water, then filter it so that the remaining sand stays as residue. (d) Evaporate the clear filtrate in a china dish (or in the sun) until the water is gone; the salt is left. (e) The salt is dissolved in the water, so it can only be recovered by evaporation after all the insoluble parts have been removed; otherwise they would be left mixed with the salt.
s: Part (a): chickpeas by hand (or strainer), being large and easy to see
Part (b): magnetic separation of the pins
Part (c): sedimentation, decantation and filtration of the sand
Part (d): evaporation of the filtrate
Part (e): dissolved salt comes last, after the insoluble parts are removed

questions.q:
Two groups were each given 100 g of a dry mixture of 15 g iron filings, 50 g sand and 35 g common salt.
Group A used a magnet on the dry mixture first, then added water, filtered and evaporated. They recovered 15 g iron, 49 g sand and 34 g salt.
Group B added water and filtered first, then used a magnet on the wet residue, then evaporated the filtrate. They recovered 13 g iron, 51 g 'sand' and 34 g salt.
(a) What percentage of the mixture is salt?
(b) Why did both groups need evaporation to get the salt?
(c) Group B's 'sand' weighed more than Group A's sand. Explain the most likely reason.
(d) Group B does not want to start again. Describe what they should do with their 51 g of 'sand' to finish the job, and give the masses of iron and clean sand they would then have.
questions.a: (a) 35 / 100 = 35%. (b) The salt was dissolved in the water and passed through the filter, so only evaporation could leave it behind as a solid. (c) The magnet picked up only 13 g of iron from the wet residue, so about 2 g of iron filings stayed mixed with Group B's sand (49 g of sand + 2 g of iron = 51 g). (d) Dry the 51 g of 'sand' fully and move a magnet through it again: the iron filings are attracted and the sand is not, so about 2 g of iron comes out. They would then have 13 + 2 = 15 g of iron and 51 - 2 = 49 g of clean sand, the same as Group A. (Using the magnet while the sand is still wet would again leave filings trapped.)
s: Part (a): 35%
Part (b): dissolved salt passes the filter, evaporation needed
Part (c): about 2 g of iron left in the sand
Part (d): dry the sand and use the magnet again, giving 15 g of iron and 49 g of sand
